title: Module Docstring: Problem Statement and Status
content: The module docstring states Erdős Problem #1053: for each $k \geq 2$, are there only finitely many $k$-perfect numbers? A $k$-perfect number satisfies $\sigma(n) = kn$ where $\sigma$ is the sum-of-divisors function. For $k = 2$ these are the classical perfect numbers (6, 28, 496, ...) characterized by the Euclid-Euler theorem. For $k \geq 3$, only finitely many examples are known. The problem connects to the Riemann Hypothesis via Gronwall's and Robin's theorems on the growth of $\sigma(n)/n$.
mathContext: A $k$-perfect number satisfies $\sigma(n) = kn$. For $k = 2$: even perfects $n = 2^{p-1}(2^p-1)$ where $2^p-1$ is a Mersenne prime (Euclid-Euler). For $k \geq 3$: only finitely many known examples, all below $10^{19}$.

title: Imports and Dependencies
content: Imports Mathlib's divisor theory (`Nat.divisors`) and basic natural number arithmetic. The `Nat.divisors` API provides the finite set of divisors of a natural number, which underpins the definition of the sum-of-divisors function $\sigma(n)$.
mathContext: The import `Mathlib.NumberTheory.Divisors` provides `Nat.divisors n`, the finset $\{d \in \mathbb{N} : d \mid n\}$, enabling $\sigma(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} d$.

title: Sum-of-Divisors Function σ(n)
content: Axiomatizes the sum-of-divisors function $\sigma(n)$ and its defining property: $\sigma(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} d$ for positive $n$. This is the fundamental multiplicative arithmetic function at the heart of perfect number theory. The multiplicativity of $\sigma$ (i.e., $\sigma(mn) = \sigma(m)\sigma(n)$ for $\gcd(m,n)=1$) is crucial for computing $\sigma$ on prime factorizations.
mathContext: $\sigma(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} d$. For a prime power, $\sigma(p^a) = \frac{p^{a+1}-1}{p-1}$. For coprime $m,n$: $\sigma(mn) = \sigma(m)\sigma(n)$.

title: k-Perfect Numbers and Perfection Multiplicity
content: Defines $n$ to be $k$-perfect when $\sigma(n) = k \cdot n$, i.e., the sum of all divisors of $n$ is exactly $k$ times $n$ itself. Also defines `perfectMultiplicity` as $\sigma(n)/n$, the abundancy index. For $k=1$ only $n=1$ qualifies; for $k=2$ these are the classical perfect numbers studied since antiquity.
mathContext: $\text{IsKPerfect}(n, k) \;:\Leftrightarrow\; n > 0 \wedge \sigma(n) = k \cdot n$. The abundancy index $I(n) = \sigma(n)/n$ satisfies $I(n) \geq 1$ with equality iff $n = 1$.

title: Uniqueness of 1-Perfect Numbers
content: States that $n = 1$ is the only 1-perfect number, i.e., the only $n$ with $\sigma(n) = n$. This is elementary: for $n > 1$, we have $\sigma(n) \geq 1 + n > n$, since $n$ has at least the divisors $1$ and $n$.
mathContext: $\sigma(n) = n \implies n = 1$, since for $n > 1$: $\sigma(n) \geq 1 + n > n$.

title: Classical Perfect Number Examples
content: States that 6, 28, 496, and 8128 are 2-perfect (classical perfect numbers). These correspond to Mersenne primes $2^p - 1$ for $p = 2, 3, 5, 7$. As of 2024, 51 even perfect numbers are known, all from Mersenne primes. Whether odd perfect numbers exist remains one of the oldest open problems in mathematics.

title: Euler's Even Perfect Number Characterization
content: The Euclid–Euler theorem: an even number $n$ is perfect if and only if $n = 2^{p-1}(2^p - 1)$ where $2^p - 1$ is a Mersenne prime. Euclid proved sufficiency (Book IX, Prop. 36, c. 300 BCE); Euler proved necessity in the 18th century. This is the only known infinite family structure among $k$-perfect numbers.

title: Triperfect Numbers (k = 3)
content: States that 120, 672, and 523776 are 3-perfect. In total, six triperfect numbers are known: 120, 672, 523776, 459818240, 1476304896, and 51001180160. It is conjectured that no others exist. The search has been exhaustive up to very large bounds.
mathContext: $\sigma(120) = 360 = 3 \cdot 120$. The six known triperfect numbers are products of small primes with carefully structured factorizations.

title: Existence of 11-Perfect Numbers
content: States the existence of a number $n$ with $\sigma(n) = 11n$. The largest known multiplicity is $k = 11$, achieved by numbers with hundreds of digits. These numbers are products of many small primes raised to carefully chosen powers. No $k = 12$ perfect number is known despite extensive computational searches.
mathContext: $\exists n \in \mathbb{N}: \sigma(n) = 11n$. Such $n$ must be divisible by many distinct primes, since $\sigma(n)/n = \prod_{p^a \| n} \frac{p^{a+1}-1}{p^a(p-1)}$.

title: Erdős Conjecture: k = o(log log n)
content: The central question of Problem #1053: if $\sigma(n) = kn$, must $k$ grow strictly slower than $\log\log n$? Formally, for any $\varepsilon > 0$, eventually $k < \varepsilon \cdot \log(\log n)$. Gronwall's theorem shows $k = O(\log\log n)$ is sharp for the supremum of $\sigma(n)/n$, so the question asks whether the integers where $\sigma(n)/n$ is exactly an integer are forced below this extremal growth rate.
mathContext: $\forall \varepsilon > 0,\; \exists N: \forall n \geq N,\; \sigma(n) = kn \implies k < \varepsilon \cdot \log(\log n)$. This is the $o(\cdot)$ formulation: $k/\log\log n \to 0$ along $k$-perfect $n$.

title: Gronwall's Theorem (1913)
content: States Gronwall's 1913 result: $\limsup_{n\to\infty} \frac{\sigma(n)}{n \log\log n} = e^\gamma$, where $\gamma \approx 0.5772$ is the Euler–Mascheroni constant. This is achieved along colossally abundant and superior highly composite numbers. It establishes $\log\log n$ as the natural scale for the growth of $\sigma(n)/n$, making Erdős's question precisely about whether $k$-perfect numbers can saturate this bound.
mathContext: $\limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{\sigma(n)}{n \log\log n} = e^\gamma \approx 1.7811$. The supremum is approached by $n = \prod_{p \leq x} p$, the primorial numbers.

title: Robin's Inequality (1984)
content: Robin's 1984 result: assuming the Riemann Hypothesis, $\sigma(n) < e^\gamma \cdot n \cdot \log\log n$ for all $n \geq 5041$. This immediately gives $k < e^\gamma \cdot \log\log n$ for $k$-perfect $n \geq 5041$, i.e., $k = O(\log\log n)$. The only known counterexamples to the unconditional version are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12, 24, and 60 — all related to colossally abundant numbers. Robin showed that his inequality is equivalent to RH.
mathContext: RH $\implies$ $\sigma(n) < e^\gamma \cdot n \cdot \log\log n$ for $n \geq 5041$. Equivalently, RH $\iff$ $\sigma(n) < e^\gamma \cdot n \cdot \log\log n$ for all $n > 5040$.

title: Guy's Finiteness Conjecture
content: Guy's conjecture from 'Unsolved Problems in Number Theory' (Problem B2): for each fixed $k \geq 3$, there exist only finitely many $k$-perfect numbers. This is strictly stronger than Erdős's $o(\log\log n)$ question — if for each $k$ the set of $k$-perfect numbers is finite, then $k$ is bounded for $k$-perfect $n$ above any threshold, which trivially implies $k = o(f(n))$ for any function $f \to \infty$.
mathContext: $\forall k \geq 3: |\{n \in \mathbb{N} : \sigma(n) = kn\}| < \infty$. This implies Erdős's conjecture since $k$ is bounded for $n$ large enough.

title: Robin's Criterion Implies O(log log n) Bound
content: Derives the $O(\log\log n)$ bound on $k$ from Robin's inequality: if $\sigma(n) = kn$ and $\sigma(n) < e^\gamma \cdot n \cdot \log\log n$, then dividing by $n$ gives $k < e^\gamma \cdot \log\log n$. This is the tightest known conditional bound. The gap between $O(\log\log n)$ (from Robin/RH) and $o(\log\log n)$ (Erdős's question) is the precise frontier of this problem.
mathContext: $\sigma(n) = kn < e^\gamma \cdot n \cdot \log\log n \implies k < e^\gamma \cdot \log\log n \approx 1.781 \cdot \log\log n$.
